extracted.intended_audience: Voters and citizens debating ratification of the U.S. Constitution (specifically the People of the State of New York)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th‑century Federalist essay arguing principles for structuring legislative authority over national defense, standing armies, and appropriations during the U.S. Constitutional ratification debates. It evaluates risks, practicalities, and institutional checks relevant to military establishment and legislative discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States keeping ships or troops without Congress's consent
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The framers of the existing Confederation...have, in express terms, prohibited them from having either ships or troops, unless with the consent of Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that separate state possession of military forces threatens the Union; gives this prohibition as an example of constitutionally sensible limits on state military power to protect national unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid restraints on national legislature's discretion in matters of common defense
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The impropriety of restraints on the discretion of the national legislature will be equally manifest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that fixed prohibitions (e.g., absolute bans on standing armies) are impractical and dangerous because they hamstring the legislature's ability to respond to contingencies; legislative discretion is necessary for national safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not absolutely prohibit RAISING armies in time of peace
rubrics_metrics.description: If prohibition is extended to the RAISING of armies in time of peace, 'the United States would then exhibit the most extraordinary spectacle...that of a nation incapacitated by its Constitution to prepare for defense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibiting the raising of armies would prevent prudent anticipatory defense measures (since formal declarations of war are infrequent); government must be able to prepare before invasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware vague prohibitions (e.g., 'keeping them up' vs 'raising')
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between raising and KEEPING THEM UP is ambiguous: 'If it be confined to the latter it will have no precise signification...When armies are once raised what shall be denominated “keeping them up”?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that imprecise wording invites evasion or inconsistent application; a poorly worded constitutional restriction will be ineffectual or easily eluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit military appropriations to two years as an effective check
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The provision contained in the new Constitution, for restraining the appropriations of money for military purposes to the period of two years'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues this is a practical safeguard: forces periodic legislative reconsideration, stimulates public debate, enables opposition and state governments to hold federal rulers to account, and prevents permanent executive military funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia alone is insufficient; a regular disciplined army is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The steady operations of war against a regular and disciplined army can only be successfully conducted by a force of the same kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites recent experience (American war) to show militia valor notwithstanding, that militias cannot by themselves establish or secure the nation; economy, stability, and effectiveness favor maintaining some regular forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing armies may be necessary in peacetime for internal security
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of Pennsylvania and Massachusetts raising troops in peace to quell disorders or preserve peace show 'cases are likely to occur...which will sometimes render a military force in time of peace essential to the security of the society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic disturbances and insurrections may require forces other than militia; blanket prohibitions on peacetime forces could prevent necessary responses to internal threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place power to raise and maintain armies in representative legislative hands, not the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: English experience showed danger when the Crown could keep troops by its own authority; the better security is referring power to the legislature: 'when they referred the exercise of that power to the judgment of the legislature, they had arrived at the ultimate point of precaution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative control (not executive unilateral authority) mitigates danger of standing forces being used to subvert liberty; representative bodies provide accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent elections and rotation reduce risk of long‑term conspiracies to usurp liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Schemes to subvert the liberties of a great community REQUIRE TIME to mature them for execution...Is it presumable, that every man...would commence a traitor...?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biennial elections and turnover in representative bodies make sustained conspiracies to build a military capable of usurpation unlikely; institutional design is a defense against gradual usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public scrutiny, opposition parties, and state legislatures will check federal military overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As often as the question comes forward, the public attention will be roused...the State legislatures...will be ready enough...to sound the alarm to the people, and not only to be the VOICE, but, if necessary, the ARM of their discontent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political contestation and intergovernmental rivalry serve as active checks: recurring defense-funding votes provide opportunities for exposure and corrective action through public opinion and state intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity of federal authority through ordinary governance reduces need for force
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The more the operations of the national authority are intermingled in the ordinary exercise of government...the greater will be the probability that it will conciliate the respect and attachment of the community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending federal powers into ordinary affairs makes the Union more legitimate and familiar, decreasing the likelihood that federal enforcement will require violent measures; broad, constructive federal activity is stabilizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union provides greater security against domestic usurpation than fragmented confederacies
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The natural strength of the people in a large community, in proportion to the artificial strength of the government, is greater than in a small...Power being almost always the rival of power, the general government will at all times stand ready to check the usurpations of the state governments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues a large, well-structured union makes popular resistance more feasible and intergovernmental checks more effective than in smaller or disunited republics; thus union mitigates risk of tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme doctrinaire restraints that render government impotent
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The idea of restraining the legislative authority...is one of those refinements which owe their origin to a zeal for liberty more ardent than enlightened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions against zealously limiting government powers in ways that undermine practical governance; pragmatic institutional design (balanced powers) is preferred to absolutist prohibitions.
